chunks: And Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated it from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan al-Luʾluʾī, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashīr, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀṣim, similarly; thus the basis regarding...

The source of these three narrations is one, and it is ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀṣim. It is possible that the intended meaning in this report is a form of recommendation rather than obligation and necessity. It is also possible that the intended meaning is that it is obligatory for him to break off if he had entered into the salat (prayer) at the beginning of the time, because we have already explained that tayammum is not permissible except at the end of the time; therefore, for that reason, breaking off became obligatory for him.

key_terms.التَّيَمُّمُ: tayammum, dry ablution used in place of wudu (ablution)
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: recommended status as opposed to strict obligation
key_terms.الِانْصِرَافُ: breaking off or withdrawing from the salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْخَبَرِ: the specific report whose legal meaning is being analyzed
key_terms.الْفَرْضِ: that which is obligatory in law

ai.seo_question: If someone begins salat (prayer) with tayammum and then finds water, must he break off the prayer?
ai.summary: This passage discusses how three reports trace back to a single narrator, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀṣim, and then explains possible legal understandings of the report. It presents two juristic possibilities: either the instruction is recommended, not obligatory, or it is obligatory to break off the salat (prayer) if one began with tayammum before the proper time for it, since tayammum is only permitted at the end of the prayer time.
